What investors fund in media now

By lowob · 13 July 2026 · 5-minute read · Strategy

Investors fund media businesses with owned audiences that pay, proprietary products those audiences need, and revenue that does not depend on a platform. Reach is the raw material, not the asset.

This is commercial advisory, not investment advice.

What stopped getting funded

Ad-supported reach was fundable when traffic was cheap and advertisers paid by volume. Neither holds now. Platforms changed their terms, programmatic rates fell, and the cost of acquiring attention rose.

Investors who backed that model carry the scars. When a media founder leads with page views and impressions, the first reaction is not interest. It is pattern recognition.

That does not mean media is unfundable. It means the thing being funded has changed. Part 3 says raise against evidence, not narrative. In media, the narrative is almost always growth in attention. The evidence is growth in money from people who chose to pay.

What gets funded

Five models attract capital in media today. Most funded companies combine two or three.

Owned audience with demonstrated willingness to pay. Paid subscriptions, memberships, premium tiers. The proof is not the list size, it is the conversion from free to paid and the renewal after the first term.

Proprietary data or research that B2B buyers pay for. Market maps, benchmarks, deal data, rankings, surveys. Buyers put these in budgets, sign annual contracts, and rarely churn if the data is used daily.

Licensing. Syndication, republication, archive access, and now content licensing to AI developers. The AI licensing market is real, but uneven: terms vary widely, demand favours depth and originality, and many publishers get no offer at all. Treat it as upside, not a plan.

Events and community with margins. Not a conference that breaks even. A programme with sponsor renewal, ticket revenue, and a cost base you can show.

Tooling or software layered on the audience. Directories, calculators, job boards, deal flow tools, databases. Software margins attached to a distribution advantage.

The evidence that counts

Most media decks lead with audience growth charts. Investors look past them to a short set of figures that describe whether the business works.

Evidence What it proves
Paid conversion rate The audience values the product enough to pay
Renewal rate They still value it after they have had it
Revenue per subscriber The economics of one relationship
Sponsor renewal rate Advertisers got results, not just impressions
Signed licensing agreements A third party has valued the content in writing
Share of revenue not platform-dependent What survives a policy change

Notice that every line is about repeat behaviour. One-off revenue tells an investor you can sell. Repeat revenue tells them you have built something.

If you cannot populate this table yet, that is your pre-raise work. Part 7 covers design partners, and in media that means your first paying cohort and your first renewing sponsors.

Alternatives to venture capital

Venture suits a small share of media businesses: those with a software layer, a large addressable B2B market, or a data product that compounds. For many others, venture terms are a poor fit for the growth rate media can deliver.

Other routes work and are often better.

Revenue-based finance: capital repaid as a share of revenue. Suits businesses with predictable subscription or sponsorship income. Strategic investors: companies that want access to your audience or data. Expect more involvement and a clearer exit path. Partnerships: a sponsor or platform funds a product line in exchange for exclusivity or first access.

Bootstrapping to profitability: slower, but you keep control and the business is sellable at any point.

Each route needs the same evidence as venture. The buyer changes, the proof does not.

Running the raise

Part 4 covers running the round like a sales process. Media founders often skip this because they are used to pitching sponsors, which is a different sale.

A sponsor buys next quarter. An investor buys the next five years. The materials need to show the model, not the audience. The data room needs the claims register from Part 2, the evidence table above, and the cohort behaviour behind it.

The most common gap I see is a strong audience and no revenue story. Fix the revenue story first. It changes who you can talk to and what they will offer.

The checklist

At least two of the five fundable models in place or in build.

Evidence table populated with your own verified numbers.

AI licensing treated as upside with no revenue dependency.

Share of revenue not dependent on platforms calculated and stated.

Venture compared against revenue-based, strategic, partnership and bootstrap routes.

Investor materials lead with repeat revenue, not audience growth.

lowob takeaways

  • Ad-supported reach stopped being fundable as platforms changed terms, programmatic rates fell and attention got more expensive.
  • AI content licensing is real but uneven; treat it as upside, not a plan.
  • A sponsor buys next quarter; an investor buys the next five years.
